title: Why Your Highlights Disappear from Memory
author: Eva Keiffenheim
summary: Eva Keiffenheim, a former school teacher who writes about learning science, diagnoses why so much of what people read fails to stick and offers a single retrieval-based habit to fix it. She opens with her own experience of reading 52 books a year and still freezing when she needed to use what she had read, arguing that reading for completion can become performative. The evidential core is a contrast between highlighting and retrieval: she cites a 2022 meta-analysis finding that highlighting gave at most a slight memory benefit and no reliable comprehension gain, and an experiment in which retrieval practice students recalled 61 percent of key ideas a week later versus 40 percent for repeated study. The practical move is to turn one useful idea per chapter into a question tied to a live situation, answer it with the book closed, check and correct, and then write a when-then intention for applying it. She closes by recommending spaced reviews at a day, a week and a month, each combining a memory test with a reflection on whether the idea has actually been used.
points: Keiffenheim argues highlighting creates an illusion of competence, citing a 2022 meta-analysis showing no reliable comprehension benefit from it.
She cites an experiment where repeated study won at five minutes but retrieval practice won at one week, with 61 percent versus 40 percent of key ideas recalled.
Her core habit is converting one idea per chapter into a small question tied to a situation the reader faces that week, answered with the book closed before checking.
Each idea gets an if-then implementation plan ("When I ___, I'll ___") so recall is linked to a concrete moment of use.
Reviews at tomorrow, next week and next month should test memory and also ask whether the idea has been applied, adjusting the plan if not.
quotes: Reading this way can become performative. You pick up a book because it’s on a list. You finish it, add it to your own list, and move on.

More importantly, marking a sentence on a page doesn’t mean you can actually use the idea in the real world. For that, you need to practice bringing the idea back to mind when the page is no longer in front of you.

In one experiment, students who repeatedly studied a short text did better on a test five minutes later. But a week later, the advantage flipped. Students who used retrieval practice—actively trying to recall the material without looking—remembered 61% of the key ideas, compared to just 40% for those who repeatedly studied it.
After finishing a chapter, pick one idea that connects to something you’re currently doing. Maybe you’re preparing for a difficult conversation, giving someone feedback, or working on a draft.

After attempting your answer, reopen the book. Check what you remembered, what you missed, and whether your example follows the advice. Correct your note. If you drew a blank, read the relevant passage, close the book, and have another go.
Remembering an idea gives you something to draw on. Using it gives you a chance to find out where it helps, what feels difficult, and what you still need to learn.
Tomorrow, next week, and next month are starting points. Write the actual dates into your note and set a reminder. If you struggle to recall the idea, check your answer and revisit it sooner.
